title: Vector SDK: Private Bots on Nostr
subtitle: Identity, channels, events, communities, encryption and operations for Vector bots, with Python labs
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on course based on the public Vector SDK documentation (vector-privacy.gitbook.io/vector-privacy/vector-sdk) and the VectorPrivacy/Vector-SDK repository. The documentation describes SDK 0.3.0 with a builder API, while the repository main branch we inspected still showed 0.2.1, so everything is presented as reported in November 2026 and you should verify the version you use. Learn how a Rust bot gets an identity, sends and reacts to messages, handles events, manages communities and invites, protects files and keys, and is troubleshot and deployed. Labs run offline and simulate the rules in Python, since Rust cannot run here.

chapters.title: What the Vector SDK is, and which version to trust
summary: The Vector SDK is a Rust library for building bots that talk over Vector, a privacy-focused messenger built on the Nostr protocol. A bot gets its own identity, can message people and communities, and reacts to events.

This course follows the public GitBook documentation, which describes SDK version 0.3.0 and says it targets Vector 0.4.0 and later. All statements are as reported in that documentation in November 2026.

The GitHub repository VectorPrivacy/Vector-SDK was found at crate version 0.2.1 on its main branch, with an older API built around VectorBot::quick. Always check which version you depend on before copying code.

glossary.def: A private messenger built on Nostr, with end-to-end encrypted direct messages and communities.
An open protocol where clients talk to relays using signed events and public keys.
A server that stores and forwards Nostr events.
A bech32 encoded public key starting with npub1; the address of a user or bot.
A bech32 encoded private key starting with nsec1; keep it secret.

keyPoints: Rust library, tokio runtime, builder API in the 0.3.0 docs.
The docs say 0.3.0 targets Vector 0.4.0 and later.
The repo main branch showed 0.2.1: verify versions before copying code.
A bot has exactly one identity per process.
Treat anything here as reported, not guaranteed.

items: ELI5. A bot is a robot mail carrier for a secret-letter club. It needs to know which version of the rulebook it has, because old and new rulebooks are different.

A messenger needs three things: a way to prove who you are, a way to send messages privately, and a way to hear about new messages. The Vector SDK gives a bot all three, so a program can take part in chats like a person would.

Under the hood it uses a crate called vector-core for encryption, networking and storage, and the nostr-sdk crate to talk to relays. It runs on tokio, Rust's asynchronous runtime, so event handlers do not block each other.

Be careful with versions. The hosted documentation presents a builder API, VectorBot::builder, and says it is version 0.3.0. The GitHub main branch we inspected still reported 0.2.1 and used a shorter VectorBot::quick entry point. Code written for one may not compile with the other.

The honest way to use any SDK is to pin an exact version, read the examples that match it, and run a small echo bot before building anything large. This course marks which API belongs to which documented version.
Everything here is about the SDK, not the Vector app itself. The documentation also covers the Concord Protocol and the messenger's own features, which this course leaves out.

practice.title: Compatible?
practice.intro: Write compatible(sdk_minor, vector_version): the docs say SDK 0.3 targets Vector 0.4.0 and later. vector_version is like '0.4.1'. Return True when sdk_minor is 3 or more and the Vector minor number is 4 or more (major 0).
practice.solution:
def compatible(sdk_minor, vector_version):
    parts = vector_version.split('.')
    major = int(parts[0])
    minor = int(parts[1])
    if sdk_minor < 3:
        return False
    return major > 0 or minor >= 4

chapters.title: Identity and keys: building a bot
summary: In the documented builder API you start with VectorBot::builder(), choose how the bot gets its keys, optionally set a data directory, and call build, which connects and returns the bot.

Keys can come from an nsec, from a mnemonic phrase, or from nothing. A keyless bot generates a key, saves it as identity.nsec in its data directory, and reuses it next time. Keys you pass in explicitly stay in memory only.
A process has one bot identity. To run more than one keyless bot on the same machine, give each its own data directory.

glossary.def: A configuration object that collects options before build creates the bot.
A list of words from which keys can be derived.
A bot built without supplied keys; it generates and persists its own.
The folder where the bot stores its state and, for keyless bots, identity.nsec.
A setting such as VECTOR_NSEC used by the examples to pass the key.

keyPoints: VectorBot::builder()...build().await? creates and connects.
Use .nsec(), .mnemonic() or leave keys out.
Keyless bots save identity.nsec in the data directory.
More than one keyless bot needs separate .data_dir() values.
bot.npub() gives the public address to share.

items: ELI5. Your bot has a public name tag anyone can read, and a secret code that only it knows. You share the name tag and hide the code.

Think of a bot as a new employee who needs a badge. The nsec is the badge's secret code, and the npub is the name on the badge that other people see. Whoever knows the secret code can act as the bot, so it must stay private.

The build call is where the bot logs in, connects to relays and syncs. Many errors such as not connected or not logged in appear when you use the bot before build has finished, so always await it first.

Without keys, the bot creates a fresh identity the first time. It writes the secret to identity.nsec in the data directory and loads it on later runs, so its address stays the same. Keys you pass explicitly are never written to disk by the SDK.
If you start two keyless bots from the same directory they would share one identity file, which is a mistake. Give each bot its own data_dir. And never commit identity.nsec or print an nsec to a log.

Read the nsec from an environment variable, as the documented examples do with VECTOR_NSEC, rather than from a source file. Rotate it by creating a new identity if you suspect it leaked, and tell your contacts the new npub.

chapters.title: Channels, messages and replies
summary: Messages go through a Channel. You get one for a direct message with bot.dm(npub), or from a chat or community with bot.channel(id), and then call methods on it.
A channel can send text, reply to a specific message, edit or delete a message, add a reaction, show that the bot is typing, and send a file from disk.
Typing indicators are short lived: the documentation describes them as expiring after 30 seconds, so a bot that is still working should send them again.

glossary.def: A conversation the bot can send to: a direct message or a community chat.
A message that points at an earlier message by its id.
An emoji attached to a message.
A temporary signal that the bot is composing a message.
A file sent with a message; it is encrypted before upload.

keyPoints: bot.dm(npub) for direct messages; bot.channel(id) for others.
send, reply, edit, delete, react, typing, send_file.
Relative file paths resolve against the working directory.
Typing hints expire after about 30 seconds.
A DM send can fail if the person has no reachable inbox relays.

items: ELI5. A channel is a door to one chat. Through the door the bot can talk, answer one particular sentence, fix its own words, add a smiley, or hand over a file.
A channel is a doorway to one conversation. Once the bot has the doorway it can speak, answer a particular earlier remark, fix a typo in its own message, or react with a thumbs up.
Replies and reactions need the id of the message they refer to. That id usually comes from an incoming message or from the result of a send, so keep it if you plan to edit or react later.

Files are encrypted before they are uploaded and a hash lets the receiver check integrity. A relative path such as report.pdf is resolved against the working directory of the process, so a service started from another folder may not find it.

Direct messages in Vector rely on the recipient's inbox relays. If the person has none that the bot can reach, the send fails with an error rather than going nowhere, and you should tell your user instead of retrying forever.
Never send private data to a channel without thinking about who is in it. In a community, everyone with access can read what the bot posts.

practice.title: Typing still showing?
practice.intro: Write typing_active(sent_at, now): a typing hint lasts 30 seconds. True when now minus sent_at is less than 30.
practice.solution:
def typing_active(sent_at, now):
    return (now - sent_at) < 30

practice.title: Keep typing alive
practice.intro: Write typing_times(duration, refresh): while the bot works for duration seconds, it re-sends typing every refresh seconds starting at 0. Return the list of times at which a hint is sent (all times below duration).
practice.solution:
def typing_times(duration, refresh):
    out = []
    t = 0
    while t < duration:
        out.append(t)
        t += refresh
    return out

practice.title: Resolve a path
practice.intro: Write resolve(cwd, path): if path starts with '/', return it; otherwise join cwd and path with a single '/' between (no double slash).

practice.title: Reply target
practice.intro: Write reply_to(messages, text): messages is a list of [id, text]. Return the id of the first message whose text equals the given text, or 'none'.

practice.title: Message chunks
practice.intro: Write chunks(text, size): split text into pieces of at most size characters and return the list. An empty text gives an empty list.
practice.solution:
def chunks(text, size):
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(text):
        out.append(text[i:i + size])
        i += size
    return out

chapters.title: Events, handlers and incoming messages
summary: Bots are event driven. You register a handler with on_message for chat messages or on_event for the wider set of events. Handlers are asynchronous and run independently, so a slow one does not block the others.
The documentation lists eight BotEvent variants: Message, MessageUpdate, Delete, MemberJoin, MemberLeave, Typing, Invite and Removed.
An IncomingMessage gives you its text, whether it is yours, its channel, and in communities the community and member. Always skip messages the bot sent itself.

glossary.def: The object passed to on_message: text, channel, sender and reply helpers.
An enum of everything a bot can be told about.
A check that tells you the bot itself sent the message.
Fetching messages that arrived while the bot was offline.
Calling the right handler for each event.

keyPoints: on_message(handler) for chat; on_event(handler) for all events.
Eight variants: Message, MessageUpdate, Delete, MemberJoin, MemberLeave, Typing, Invite, Removed.
Skip is_mine() messages to avoid loops.
The bot reconnects automatically and catches up.
Keep the process alive or no events will arrive.

items: ELI5. Events are like doorbells. Each kind of bell goes to a different helper, and the bot must not answer its own doorbell.
Imagine a switchboard operator. Calls arrive in any order, and each one is passed to the right desk. In the SDK, every incoming thing becomes an event, and your handlers are the desks.

This is the shape of the documented echo-style bot. The first check protects against loops; without it the bot would answer its own replies. After registering handlers, the main task must stay alive, for example by awaiting a signal, or the process exits and no events arrive.

on_event is for everything else. A MemberJoin lets a moderation bot greet newcomers, an Invite tells the bot it was asked to join a community, and Removed says it was taken out. Typing events are short lived signals you can usually ignore.
Because handlers run independently, do not rely on two events being processed in the order they arrived. If order matters, use ids and timestamps from the events, not the order of your code running.
If the connection drops, the SDK reconnects by itself and catches up on messages it missed, according to the docs. Your handlers should therefore be safe to run for messages that are a little old.

chapters.title: Communities, invites and members

maps.title: Communities
links: Member | can be | Kicked or banned
capabilities | tell | What bot may do

summary: A community is a shared space with members and roles. Your bot can be invited to one, read and send messages there, welcome new members, and, if it has the rights, moderate.

What happens to an invitation depends on the invite policy you set on the builder. Manual is the default and leaves invites pending until you call accept_invite. Public accepts everyone. Whitelist accepts only listed npubs and quietly ignores the rest.
Invitations that arrived while the bot was offline are accepted on startup in the automatic modes.

glossary.def: The builder setting that decides what the bot does with invitations.
A list of npubs whose invitations are accepted automatically.
A right the bot has in a community, such as kicking or banning.
A set of rights given to members, such as admin.
The member who created the community; only they can dissolve it.

keyPoints: Default policy is Manual: use pending_invites() and accept_invite(&id).
Public accepts anyone; Whitelist accepts only listed npubs and silently ignores others.
Check community.capabilities() before kick or ban.
dissolve() is owner only and cannot be undone.
sync_communities() refreshes stale ids.

items: ELI5. A community is a clubhouse. A bot can be told to say yes to every invitation, only to friends on a list, or to ask a grown-up each time.

Think of a club that sends your bot a membership card. Manual policy means a person looks at each card first. Public policy means the bot joins any club that asks. Whitelist means it only joins clubs run by people on a list.

In the whitelist mode, invitations from anyone else are silently ignored; the sender gets no refusal message. For a public helper bot you choose Public, but then anyone can add it to a community, so consider what it will do there.

Once inside, a community gives you member lists, roles, and methods to edit the name and description, create invites or leave. A Member can be asked for its profile, and checked with is_owner and is_admin.

Moderation actions such as kick and ban need admin rights. The bot should check capabilities first instead of trying and failing. Dissolve is the most destructive action: only the owner may call it, and it cannot be undone, so a bot should never do it without a person confirming.
If an id you stored no longer works, the bot's local view is stale. Run sync_communities to refresh it before assuming the community is gone.

chapters.title: Privacy, encryption and security practice
summary: The documentation says files are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and verified with a SHA-256 hash, and that direct messages use NIP-59 gift wrapping. Reactions use NIP-25, typing indicators use NIP-40 expiry, and inbox relays use NIP-17.
Privacy still has limits. Relays can withhold or delay messages, profile data is public, and if a key is compromised, past messages could be exposed.
Good practice follows from that: never hardcode or commit keys, use wss relays, cap file sizes, keep logs free of sensitive data, rotate keys on a schedule, and report vulnerabilities privately.

glossary.def: An authenticated encryption mode; it hides content and detects tampering.
A hash function used to check that data did not change.
A Nostr technique that hides who is talking to whom inside an outer envelope.
A websocket connection protected by TLS.
An anonymity network that hides your network address; optional in the SDK through a feature.

keyPoints: Do not commit keys; use environment variables.
Use wss:// relays only.
Cap file sizes and avoid logging sensitive content.
A compromised key can expose old messages; rotate every 6 to 12 months.
Report vulnerabilities privately; the team acknowledges within 48 hours.

items: ELI5. Files are put in a locked box with a seal. If the seal is broken the box is not trusted. Remember, the post office can see that a box came, even if it cannot open it.

Imagine sending a letter inside a locked box, then inside a plain envelope with a fake return address. The box hides the contents, the outer envelope hides who is writing to whom. That is the idea behind encrypted files and gift-wrapped direct messages.

AES-256-GCM uses a 256-bit key, which is 32 bytes. The GCM mode also adds an authentication tag, conventionally 16 bytes, so the encrypted data is longer than the original by that amount, and any change to it is detected when decrypting.
The SHA-256 hash is like a fingerprint. If a downloaded file does not match the fingerprint that came with it, it was damaged or tampered with, and the bot should refuse to use it.

Be honest about limits. A relay can see that something arrived even if it cannot read it, and can drop or delay messages. Profile information such as a name is public. And since keys do not expire on their own, losing one can expose history.

Tor needs both the Cargo feature and the tor call. Without the feature the call has no effect, so test that it really takes effect rather than assuming it did. Startup is slower because the embedded client has to bootstrap during build.

chapters.title: Example bots: echo, slash, AI, moderation, files

maps.title: Examples
links: moderation_bot | welcomes and bans | By word filter

summary: The documentation ships a set of example bots: echo_bot, slash_command_bot, ai_bot, moderation_bot, whitelist_bot, file_bot and save_files_bot. All need the VECTOR_NSEC environment variable, and you start one with cargo run -p vector-sdk --example name.

The slash_command_bot handles /ping, /echo, /roll and /help by parsing message text, since these are bot-side conventions in a chat, not a server feature. The ai_bot calls an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, shows a typing indicator, replies in threads and keeps a history per chat.
It needs OPENAI_API_KEY.
The moderation_bot welcomes members on MemberJoin and bans on a word filter.

glossary.def: A small runnable program in the repository that shows one feature.
A message starting with a slash that the bot parses itself.
The list of earlier messages sent to a language model as context.
A rule that matches banned words in a message.
The environment variable the AI example expects for its model endpoint.

keyPoints: cargo run -p vector-sdk --example echo_bot with VECTOR_NSEC set.
slash_command_bot: /ping, /echo, /roll, /help.
ai_bot needs OPENAI_API_KEY and keeps per-chat history.
moderation_bot: welcome on MemberJoin, ban on filtered words.
Run examples with a throwaway identity first.

items: ELI5. The example bots are little practice robots: one repeats, one follows commands, one chats, one keeps order. Always practise with a pretend identity.
The best way to learn an SDK is to run its smallest program. The echo bot receives a message and sends the same text back. It touches the whole path: identity, connection, event, reply.

lesson.code:
# in a shell (names as reported in the examples page)
export VECTOR_NSEC='nsec1...'   # use a throwaway identity
cargo run -p vector-sdk --example echo_bot

items: The command bot adds parsing: split the text at the first space, look at the command word, and act. The documented set is ping, echo, roll and help, and anything else gets the help text.

The AI bot is the largest example. For each incoming message it shows typing, sends the conversation so far to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and replies. Keep the history short, because long histories cost money and slow replies.

The moderation bot shows why handlers need care. A filter that bans on a single word will punish innocent people; a careful bot warns first, logs the reason without the message text, and leaves final decisions to admins.
Before pointing any example at a real community, run it in a private test chat with a throwaway key, and read its source so you know exactly what it will do with the permissions you give it.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting, tracing and deployment

maps.title: Operations
links: Not connected | means | build not finished
No events | means | Process not alive
Bunker signer | cannot do | Concord rekeys

summary: Most problems fall into a few families. A not connected or not logged in error means you used the bot before build finished. A DM send failure usually means no reachable inbox relays. A stale id means run sync_communities.

If on_message never fires, keep the process alive and message the printed npub from another account. If kick or ban fails, check capabilities. If send_file cannot find a file, check the working directory. Turn on debug logging with RUST_LOG=vector_sdk=debug.
In production run the bot under a supervisor, keep secrets out of logs, and monitor reconnect storms.

keyPoints: Await build() before any other call.
No events? Keep the process alive and message the printed npub.
RUST_LOG=vector_sdk=debug for detail.
Check capabilities before moderation; run sync_communities for stale ids.
Supervise, log without secrets, back off on retries.

items: ELI5. When a toy will not work, check the cheap things first: is it switched on, are the batteries in, did the setup finish, and is anyone listening?

When something fails, work from the cheapest check to the dearest. First, is the process running and did build finish? Second, is the key right? Third, can the target be reached? Only then read deeper logs.

lesson.code:
# turn on debug output (name as given in the troubleshooting page)
RUST_LOG=vector_sdk=debug cargo run -p vector-sdk --example echo_bot

items: A classic mistake is registering a handler and then letting main return. The program ends, the connection closes and nothing is ever delivered. Wait on a signal or a channel so the process stays alive.
A second classic is a relative path. A service started by systemd runs from another folder than your shell, so report.pdf is not where you thought. Use absolute paths in services.

For retries use exponential backoff with a cap and some randomness, so a fleet of bots does not stampede a relay after an outage. Treat authentication errors differently from network errors: do not retry a bad key.

Deploy under systemd or a container with a restart policy. Give each bot its own data directory, protect the directory with file permissions, and keep a runbook: how to rotate the key, how to read logs, and who to tell.

practice.title: Backoff with cap
practice.intro: Write waits(n, base, cap): return the first n retry waits; the first is base, each next doubles, never above cap.
practice.solution:
def waits(n, base, cap):
    out = []
    w = base
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(min(w, cap))
        w = w * 2
    return out
